# Week in Review: November 23, 2026


November 23, 2026


#### Summary


- Equity markets suffer worst week since April 2025.
- Anthropic initial public offering (IPO) sets record for largest in history.
- 10-Year Treasury yield back below 5% as investors seek safe haven assets.


#### Overview


Markets suffered their worst week since April 2025, dragged lower by a sharp selloff in artificial intelligence (AI) related stocks. The selloff was driven by the culmination of multiple factors, some of which had been brewing for months- concerns about the potential returns on the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent by AI hyperscalers, higher interest rates, possible additional Fed rate hikes- and others which had appeared more recently- Nvidia scandal and ensuing fallout, political opposition to data centers crystalized by midterm elections results. The Philly Semiconductor Sector Index, widely viewed as a proxy for the AI industry, ended the week down 17.1%, including a 10.7% decline on Friday. The index is now down 42.5% from its record high set in late June.


Though the week’s selloff was jarring, especially given the overall lack of volatility experienced thus far in 2026, it was a reminder that no bull market is linear, and even the strongest experience pullbacks, commonly referred to as consolidations. While these episodes can be painful, they often serve as the starting point for the market’s next upward ascent. Given the uncertainties facing AI stocks, it is too soon to know if the current pullback is a consolidation within a longer bull market, or the first leg down of a bear market. Investors looking for a silver lining can take comfort in the fact that since 1950 the S&P 500 has always been positive 12 months after a midterm election with an average gain of nearly 15%. While the historical pattern could once again repeat, it does not preclude the possibility of additional near-term volatility.


The initial post-election selloff didn’t seem like the final selloff. Necessary, but insufficient. While AI had been under pressure for several months, given how much “froth” was in the markets, surrounding AI names, and how many were “priced for perfection” a one-day selloff didn’t seem sufficient to really reset investors’ expectations. Felt like more of an overture to a larger selloff that finally materialized this past week.


Despite Anthropic IPO, what little excitement it kindled, quickly dissipated, as investors continued to sell previously high-flying AI, and AI related stocks. Reflected in the performance of the tech-heavy NASDAQ which fell % for the week to end firmly in correction territory (down 10% or more from record high) ending the week down X% from its record high set in X. Selloff was even more evident in the performance of the Philly Semiconductor index which fell X% and to end the week Y% below its all-time high set in X%.


Consumer spending measured by headline retail sales slowed in October, increasing just 0.2% for the month, following September’s 0.8% gain. The deceleration was led by a 1.8% decline in automobile sales, a 2.3% decline in furniture and home furnishing sales, and restaurant sales growth of just 0.2%, down from September’s 0.9% increase. Despite the slower headline figure, control sales, a more core measure of the headline figure, which factor into the calculation of GDP, rose 0.6%, an encouraging sign for fourth quarter GDP growth.


Through Friday, 93% of S&P 500 companies reported 3Q26 earnings. Thus far, 84% have beaten their consensus estimate. According to industry group FactSet, consolidated S&P 500 earnings growth for the quarter is expected to be 33%, led for the first time since 4Q22 by the other 493 companies in the index, not the Mag 7. Mag 7 earnings growth for the quarter is expected to be 27%.


#### The Details


**Equities**


Equities finally succumbed to the pressure building below the surface of the market over recent months, with the major indices having their worst week since the post-tariff meltdown in April 2025. The S&P 500 fell 8.6% for the week while the Nasdaq fell 10%. The S&P 500 Equal Weight and Russell 2000 (small caps) declined 6.2% and 7.4%, respectively, for the week—a big fall but considerably less than the more tech-heavy indices. The S&P 500 is now down 10% from its all-time-high, marking a “correction” for the index, after falling seven consecutive days. International markets were also under pressure, with the MSCI EAFE down 6.3%. The US market’s stress indicator, the VIX, shot up 57% for the week to 35.9. Readings above 30 tend to indicate an extremely high level of short-term stress.


In a positive sign for the US consumer, Walmart reported healthy earnings with good growth and profitability, and management reporting that the consumer is stable and resilient while the company held goods pricing growth to only 1-2%. While a solid data point for the broader economy, investors were once again more focused on the engine for the economy at the moment, AI. Embattled AI belle weather, Nvidia, reported strong third quarter earnings and raised forward guidance. However, with more questions than answers about its future accumulating without co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, and rumors of an accounting investigation by the SEC on Friday, investors were more inclined to exit rather than reward the current strong earnings.


In what should have been an encouraging event for AI confidence, leading frontier lab company, Anthropic, completed its much-anticipated initial public offering (IPO), raising over $100B at a price above expectations, with demand exceeding available shares for sale multiple times. The shares traded higher on the first day of trading but fell back toward the IPO price amidst the market carnage on Friday.


Strong third quarter earnings from Walmart, Nvidia and Anthropic suggest that the Main Street and AI economies are *currently* in good health. But markets are looking forward and continue to grow more concerned; the current strength is not sustainable. The scale and pace of AI investment is unprecedented. Interest rates are rising. With a clear memory of past busts and few analogs to compare this cycle against, markets are applying greater scrutiny to forward expectations. Investors express uncertainty by applying a lower multiple to expected future earnings, thus improving the margin of safety against possible disappointment. In the case of the S&P 500, the 2027 PE ratio has fallen to 16.2x, near the lowest level of the last ten years.


Diverging trends had been swirling beneath the surface of the market for months, with AI and non-AI stocks moving in different directions. A narrow market such as this tends to be unstable and thus unsustainable, as discussed in prior Weeks in Review. These conditions typically resolve with the broader market moving lower in what can be a clearing event, planting the seeds for another market advance. Little is likely to be cleared up regarding AI market leader Nvidia over the near term and investors are also watching interest rates and Fed policy closely. Thus, equity markets are likely to remain volatile over the coming weeks. Beyond the near-term, it is too soon to declare if this is a pause that refreshes ahead of another market advance. While the facts can always change, current fundamentals are clearly strong; energy and other commodity prices are moving down, and some exuberance has been cleared from the equity markets. These conditions could tilt the balance of risks and opportunities positively over the coming six months.


**Fixed Income**


Fixed income regained much of the ground it lost the prior week as renewed concerns surrounding the AI trade and broader equity market weakness drove investors back into Treasuries. The 10-Year Treasury yield declined 21bps to 4.94%, moving back below the closely watched 5% level. The 2-Year yield fell 23bps to 4.65%, while the 30-Year declined 14bps to 5.33%. Yields moved gradually lower through much of the week before Friday’s equity selloff accelerated the flight to quality. The reversal was particularly notable given that inflation concerns and expectations for additional Fed rate hikes remain firmly in place.


Wednesday’s release of the October FOMC meeting minutes reinforced the Fed’s hawkish stance. Almost all participants believed additional tightening would likely be necessary to bring inflation back toward the Fed’s 2% target, with a couple even suggesting an increase greater than 25bps could warrant consideration if inflation remains elevated. Fed Governor Lisa Cook echoed those concerns Friday, arguing that current financial conditions remain too accommodative. Despite the increasingly hawkish commentary, markets ended the week pricing in a 92% probability of a 25bp hike at the December meeting. The Treasury rally highlighted an interesting dynamic; investors were willing to move into government bonds for safety even as the outlook for monetary policy remains restrictive.


Economic data provided some additional support for lower yields. October retail sales rose just 0.2%, slowing from September’s 0.8% increase, while industrial production declined 0.4% following a 0.7% increase in the previous month. Initial jobless claims remained relatively stable at 203K, suggesting the labor market has yet to show meaningful deterioration. Oil prices also continued to ease, offering some relief from the inflation pressures that have dominated the bond market for much of the year. Taken together the softer economic readings and declining risk appetite outweighed concerns about further Fed tightening, at least for the week.


In credit, investment grade issuance remained elevated, with 33 borrowers bringing approximately $52B of new bonds to market, exceeding the $35B initially expected. Year to date issuance now stands near $1.97T. Unlike the resilience demonstrated in recent weeks, investment grade spreads widened roughly 6bps through Thursday as equity market weakness and concerns surrounding AI-related financing weighed on sentiment. High yield spreads experienced greater pressure reflecting increased sensitivity to broader risk appetite. Despite the widening, the investment grade market continued to absorb substantial supply. The divergence between falling Treasury yields and widening credit spreads suggests investors are becoming more selective about the risks they are willing to take.


Municipal bonds participated in the broader fixed income rally but generally lagged Treasuries. 10-Year AAA municipal yields declined approximately 15bps to 3.25%, compared with the 23bps decline in the 10-year Treasury, leaving the muni/treasury ratio near 66%. Fund flows continued to present a mixed picture, with municipal mutual fund redemptions offset by demand for municipal ETFs as investors repositioned portfolios and continued tax loss harvesting activity. Although November’s technical backdrop has generally been supportive, heavy issuance and shifting fund flows have limited some of the market’s relative strength. The new issue calendar is expected to slow, so the balance between supply and reinvestment demand will remain an important driver of municipal performance heading into December.
